hook: Did you know archaeologists found ancient mummies buried with golden tongues while searching for Cleopatra's lost tomb?
article: In twenty twenty-one, a team searching for Cleopatra at Taposiris Magna announced the discovery of mummies with golden tongues. This ruined temple stands thirty miles west of Alexandria, where excavators also uncovered twenty-seven tombs and ten mummies.

Searchers found more than three hundred coins from her lifetime and a bust of a man with a cleft chin that looks a lot like Mark Antony. A foundation plate showed that the temple was dedicated to the goddess Isis, and Cleopatra saw herself as the living Isis.
Imagine standing inside a desert temple where mummies were left with gold inside their mouths. Even with these unbelievable discoveries, no one has proven that the queen's tomb is actually there.
engage: What detail from this temple search surprised you the most?
author: KevinDInno

hook: How did ancient builders align a mountain temple so the sun reaches an inner sanctuary over sixty meters deep only twice a year?
article: Far inside the mountain, at the very end of the temple, four gods sit together in the dark. On two mornings each year, in February and in October, the rising sun lines up perfectly with the temple's doorway.

The beam of light travels more than sixty meters deep into the rock to illuminate the seated statues of Amun, Ra-Horakhty, and the king himself. But Ptah, a god connected with the underworld, remains completely in shadow.

For three thousand years, that mysterious moment repeated deep inside the mountain with nobody left to explain it. Today, even after the entire structure was saved and relocated, crowds still gather from around the world as the sun finds its way inside.
engage: Would you find the precise solar alignment sixty meters deep or the deliberate shadowing of the underworld god more impressive to see in person?
author: Diego Delso

hook: Did you know an ancient pharaoh flew on an airplane over three thousand years after his death?
article: In September of nineteen seventy-six, more than three thousand years after his death, the mummy of Ramesses the Second flew to Paris for conservation work. The ancient king remained there until returning to Egypt the following May.

You may have heard that he was given a passport for the flight, but that famous story is not true. Long before his modern journey, ancient priests had moved his body to a hidden shaft to protect it from tomb robbers until eighteen eighty-one.
Today, Ramesses rests in Cairo where visitors from around the world can stand face to face with him. Standing before his mummy allows you to meet a king who ruled Egypt for sixty-six years.
engage: Did you previously believe the famous rumor that the pharaoh was given a modern passport?
author: Rodolfo Valverde

hook: Did you know that silver was once considered far more valuable than gold in ancient Egypt?
article: During Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, silver was considerably rarer and more valuable than gold because it had to be imported. When French Egyptologist Pierre Montet stepped into the undisturbed burial chamber of Pharaoh Psusennes I in February 1940, he discovered the king interred inside a breathtaking silver coffin inlaid with solid gold.

Lower Egypt's extremely humid climate destroyed all perishable wooden artifacts inside the tomb, but the breathtaking metal treasures remained entirely preserved. Over his mummy lay a funerary mask of solid gold and lapis lazuli, while his body was adorned with solid gold sandals and gold finger stalls complete with sculpted fingernails.

Despite rivaling the famous intact tomb of Tutankhamun, this astonishing royal breakthrough was largely swallowed from history because World War II erupted at the exact same moment. Seeing these exquisite gold and silver treasures today reminds us of the massive wealth that lay hidden underground while the world stood on the brink of destruction.
engage: Would you have guessed that ancient Egyptians prized imported silver even more than gold?
author: Aidan McRae Thomson

hook: Did you know ancient Egyptian royal wigs were crafted with over a thousand individual gold rings?
article: Royal princesses wore intricate wigs adorned with 1,251 gold rings, creating a shimmering effect as they moved through the court. Princess Sithathoriunet's wig was reconstructed to show how these gold stripes caught the desert sunlight.

The princesses also used cosmetic vessels to store black kohl derived from galena to darken their eyes and protect them from infection. A study suggests the lead in their makeup actually helped boost nitric oxide, preventing eye diseases.

Today, these treasures stand as a testament to Middle Kingdom artistry and the luxurious lives of the royal princesses. As the light catches the carnelian and lapis, we are reminded of the humans who once wore them.
engage: Which detail of ancient Egyptian royal beauty care surprised you the most?
author: Unknown

hook: Did you know ancient Egypt's highest military award for battlefield bravery was a set of golden flies?
article: In 1859, excavators unburied the sealed wooden coffin of Queen Ahhotep containing three glittering golden flies. While ordinary housefly amulets were popular symbolic items, actual golden flies served as the military's highest award for battlefield bravery.

Remarkably, none of the fourteen fine inscribed artifacts found inside the coffin actually bore Queen Ahhotep's own name. Five objects explicitly bore the name of King Kamose, while seven items were attributed to the young pharaoh Ahmose I.

These golden flies stood as an eternal symbol of persistent, unyielding military service on the battlefield. Though her physical mummy was destroyed after discovery, these precious artifacts endure as an ultimate badge of ancient combat bravery.
engage: What detail surprised you most about a royal queen being buried with battlefield bravery awards?
author: Rob Corder
